g-conditional-07.reason: Real future condition: If + present simple (reaches), main clause will resume. B 'will reach' is the classic if+will trap; here will is neither willingness nor a result, so a formal editor changes it. D 'would reach' is unreal/willingness, wrong for an inanimate shipment with a will main clause. C 'reached' needs the unstated assumption that Friday has already passed (real past condition).
g-conditional-07.ldbs: L yes (will reach / reached both read fine in 'shipment ... ___ the plant'); D yes (If is 16 words before the blank, 'will resume' after); B no (if+will is well-known to good students); S weak. Fails B, so not hard.
g-conditional-07.why: Medium: L and D pass, but the if+will trap is one good students already know (B fails).
g-conditional-07.fix: B 'will reach' and C 'reached' are only weak competitors; to remove the 'reached = already past' reading, replace C with 'had reached' (or 'reaching').
g-conditional-07.editorNote: C 'reached' (real past, speaker already past Friday) and B 'will reach' (if + predicted future event, BrE tolerates when the clause is a premise) both need an extra assumption or are marginal; not enough for mustFix, but better replaced.

g-conditional-08.reason: Logic: the block is released to the public unless the coordinator has confirmed. 'if' and 'as long as' reverse the logic (release if confirmed). 'in case' = as a precaution against, which does not fit 'has confirmed'. No alternative reading holds.
g-conditional-08.ldbs: L yes ('public, if the coordinator has confirmed' reads fine locally); D yes (the logic is set by 'release it to the general public' and 'by that date'); B weak (if/unless swap is a real trap but the logic is easy to check); S weak.
g-conditional-08.why: Medium: L and D pass, B is only moderate because the unless/if logic check is one step.
g-conditional-08.editorNote: Batch note: this answer 'unless' is a distractor in g-conditional-09 and 'as long as' here duplicates the answer family of 09 ('provided that').

g-conditional-09.reason: Keep entitlements on condition that she transfers before January: provided that. 'unless' reverses the logic; 'in case' = precaution, no; 'until' contradicts 'forfeit both if she waits'.
g-conditional-09.ldbs: L yes (unless/until/provided that all read locally); D yes (the but-clause 'forfeit both if she waits' is 13+ words after); B weak; S no.
g-conditional-09.why: Medium: L and D pass; the second clause nearly spells out the logic, so B is weak.
g-conditional-09.editorNote: Tail 'but she will forfeit both if she waits until the new year' half-defines the answer (style 3). Batch: 'unless' (distractor here) is the answer of 08; 'in case' repeats from 08.

g-conditional-10.reason: unless + present simple for a future event: 'unless the rain stops'. B 'does not stop' double-negates (moved unless the rain does not stop = moved if it stops, absurd). A 'will stop': unless + will is not used for a simple prediction. D past simple is unreal/backshift, but the main clause is will.
g-conditional-10.ldbs: L yes (will stop / does not stop both read locally); D yes (unless is 11 words before the blank across a relative clause); B moderate (unless+will, unless+not are common errors, but good students know them); S moderate.
g-conditional-10.why: Medium: L and D pass, B only moderate because unless+present is a well-drilled rule.

g-conditional-11.reason: Intended: unreal present 'were' + would. But A 'is' gives a real condition with a hypothetical 'would be cleared' main clause ('If the center is able to run a second shift, its backlog would be cleared'), a pattern grammars accept (if + present, would = tentative consequence). The 'but the council will not fund the extra staff' clause does not force the unreal reading: the center's ability is still an open question, so the sentence stays coherent and no extra assumption is needed. Accepted in BrE and AmE formal writing, though an editor might prefer 'will be cleared'.
g-conditional-11.ldbs: L yes ('center ... is able' fine); D yes (would be cleared is 9+ words after); B no (If...were...would is the standard form everyone knows); S weak. Fails B.
g-conditional-11.why: Medium: L and D pass but B fails; and the second answer undermines it anyway.
g-conditional-11.fix: Make the condition known to be false so that 'is' becomes incoherent: e.g. '..., its backlog would be cleared by December, but the center has only one crew and the council has refused to fund a second.' Alternatively add 'at present it cannot' before the if-clause.
g-conditional-11.editorNote: Real vs unreal readings both fit the facts as given.

g-conditional-12.reason: Second conditional: if its agents had ... would resolve; 'at present' confirms present unreal. B will resolve and D has resolved mismatch with 'had'. C 'would have resolved' mismatches if + past simple; not standard in formal English.
g-conditional-12.ldbs: L yes (would have resolved reads fine near the blank); D yes (if-clause and 'at present' follow the 10-word predicate); B no; S no.
g-conditional-12.why: Medium: L and D pass, but no distractor that good students actively believe; if-clause is fairly visible.

g-conditional-13.reason: Third conditional: If + had identified ... would have been avoided. A 'identified' (past simple) is nonstandard in a past counterfactual, and as a real past condition it would contradict the fact that the cancellations happened. B and D are ungrammatical in an if-clause.
g-conditional-13.ldbs: L yes (all four fit 'center ___ the crew shortage'); D yes (would have been avoided is at the very end); B weak (past simple for past hypothetical is a common learner error, but good students know); S no.
g-conditional-13.why: Medium: L and D pass; B weak because third conditional is the most drilled pattern.
g-conditional-13.editorNote: A 'identified' needs a strained deduction reading (if it did identify it...), which the known fact of the cancellations contradicts; fine as a trap.

g-conditional-14.reason: Mixed conditional: past unreal condition (had accepted in 2019), present result ('now, seven years later'): would be. A 'would have been ... now' is a pure third-conditional pattern with a present state; informal at best, an editor would change it to 'would be'. C will be and D had been are wrong.
g-conditional-14.ldbs: L yes ('reading room would have been the busiest' fine locally); D yes ('now, seven years later' is the last 5 words, after the blank + 7 words); B yes (the 'had accepted' primes strongly toward would have been); S yes (recognize it as mixed, identify time reference of the result clause).
g-conditional-14.why: Hard: L, D, B and S all pass; the time reference is set only by 'now, seven years later' at the end, against the 'had accepted' priming.
g-conditional-14.editorNote: A 'would have been ... now' is heard colloquially ('would have been a doctor now') but is not standard formal; legitimate trap.

g-conditional-15.reason: Mixed: present unreal state (were not dependent) with past result (would not have been disrupted by the strike that ended last Monday). A 'would not be' matches the if-clause form and could read as continuing disruption after the strike, but the sentence does not say the disruption is ongoing; 'ended last Monday' + 'so badly disrupted by the strike' reads as a completed past effect. B and C are wrong in the main clause.
g-conditional-15.ldbs: L yes (would not be / would not have been both read fine near the blank); D yes ('strike that ended last Monday' is 8 words after the blank); B yes (would not be mirrors 'were not'; strong pull); S yes (mixed conditional, read time off the result clause).
g-conditional-15.why: Hard: L, D, B and S pass; the past time of the result is given only by 'strike that ended last Monday'.
g-conditional-15.fix: Close the 'continuing disruption' reading by adding a past anchor: '... so badly disrupted last month by the strike that ended last Monday.'
g-conditional-15.editorNote: A 'would not be so badly disrupted by the strike that ended last Monday' is grammatical if the disruption is still ongoing after the strike (aftermath). Requires an extra assumption, so not ambiguous, but near.

g-conditional-16.reason: 'But for + noun' = if it had not been for; fits would have been forced. B 'Because of' is the wrong direction (the loan did not cause closure). A Whereas and D Unless cannot take a noun phrase.
g-conditional-16.ldbs: L yes ('Because of the emergency loan' reads fine); D yes (would have been forced is 13+ words later); B weak (Because of is excluded by meaning easily); S no.
g-conditional-16.why: Medium: L and D pass; B fails because the logic of the main clause rules out Because of at once; the difficulty is just knowing 'but for'.
g-conditional-16.editorNote: Unit note: 'but for' and 'without' (item 17) are the same point.

g-conditional-17.reason: Without + noun, present reference ('as it does at present'): would not be. B 'would not have been able to keep its galleries open ... as it does at present' is a stretch: could be read as 'the museum would not have been able to start/keep this up over the years', but it needs an extra assumption about a past decision. C past perfect and D future perfect are wrong.
g-conditional-17.ldbs: L yes (would not have been fits 'museum ___ able to keep'); D yes ('as it does at present' is 13 words later); B moderate; S no. The 'at present' tail is a textbook marker.
g-conditional-17.why: Medium: L and D pass; B moderate at most; the answer is signaled by 'at present'.
g-conditional-17.fix: Replace B 'would not have been' with 'is not' (excluded by 'as it does') or add a past-excluding marker.
g-conditional-17.editorNote: B can be read as past-continuing hypothetical ('would not have been able to keep open ... as it does'), needing an assumption; shouldFix.

g-conditional-18.reason: Should + subject + bare verb ('fail'): inverted 'if ... should'. A If would need 'fails' (If ... fail is an archaic subjunctive that a formal editor would change); C Would makes a question; D Unless cannot take would shut down logic here.
g-conditional-18.ldbs: L yes (If / Would read fine at the start); D yes (bare 'fail' is 14 words after the blank, past a relative clause); B weak (nobody keeps 'If' once they see bare 'fail'); S yes but thin. Not enough B.
g-conditional-18.why: Medium: L and D pass, S thin, B fails.
g-conditional-18.editorNote: A 'If ... fail' (present subjunctive) survives in archaic legal drafting only; fine here, not flagged.

g-conditional-19.reason: Inversion with 'be': Were + subject + not due to expire. If/Had/Should cannot be followed by a verb-less 'not due'.
g-conditional-19.ldbs: L yes (each head reads fine before 'the lease'); D yes ('not due' follows a relative clause, 17 words after); B no (nobody believes 'If ... not due'); S thin (the cue is the missing be-verb).
g-conditional-19.why: Medium: L and D pass, but no distractor is believable once 'not due' is read.
g-conditional-19.editorNote: Batch: items 18-21 are four consecutive inversion items with the same option set permuted (answers of one are distractors of another); vary the unit.

g-conditional-20.reason: Had + subject + p.p. (received). B and C are not past participles; D 'have received' (Had he have received) is dialectal/colloquial, not formal.
g-conditional-20.ldbs: L yes (every form fits a verb slot after 'August,'); D yes ('Had' is 13 words before); B weak ('have received' is an informal/spoken form); S thin.
g-conditional-20.why: Medium: L and D pass; no distractor a good student believes. The relative clause is filler.
g-conditional-20.editorNote: Only tests Had + p.p.; the insertion adds length but no real obstacle.

g-conditional-21.reason: The sentence already has 'had approved' as the finite verb, so the opener must be If (not an inversion). Had / Should / Were + 'had approved' would give a double verb.
g-conditional-21.ldbs: L yes ('Had the planning tribunal' reads fine locally); D yes ('had approved' is 8 words after the blank, behind the insertion); B yes (inversion reflex: Had in a third-conditional sentence is a strongly believed form, boosted by the 'had repeatedly requested' in the insertion); S yes (find the main verb past the insertion).
g-conditional-21.why: Hard: L, D, B and S pass; a reverse-inversion trap (the answer is the plain If).

g-conditional-22.reason: 'If only' + past simple = unreal wish about the present: had a larger loading area, trucks would not have to queue. A 'has' (hope/real) does not match the would main clause; C 'would have' is for others' behavior/annoyance and doesn't fit an inanimate venue; D will have is wrong.
g-conditional-22.ldbs: L yes (has / had both fine in 'venue, which opened in 1998, ___ a larger'); D yes ('would not have to queue' is 8 words after; 'If only' is 12 before); B weak (If only + present is not a form good students believe); S thin.
g-conditional-22.why: Medium: L and D pass; B weak. The past-tense 'opened in 1998' pushes toward 'had', if anything.

g-conditional-23.reason: It is high time that + past simple (reviewed) for a present-time wish. A 'reviews' is the near miss: 'It is high time that the government takes action' occurs in editorials, but prescriptive/formal usage requires the past form after 'high time', and an editor would normally change it. B will review and D is reviewing are wrong.
g-conditional-23.ldbs: L yes (reviews / reviewed both fit after 'has fallen ...,'); D yes ('It is high time that' is 15 words before the blank); B yes (the present-perfect 'has fallen' pulls toward present 'reviews'); S yes (skip the whose-clause to connect to 'high time').
g-conditional-23.why: Hard: L, D, B and S pass.
g-conditional-23.fix: Replace A 'reviews' with 'has reviewed' to remove the attested 'it is high time ... takes' usage.
g-conditional-23.editorNote: A 'reviews': present indicative after 'it is high time that' is attested in British and American editorial prose; not mustFix, but a risk.

g-conditional-24.reason: as though + unreal present: were. C 'had been' is for an unreal past; the evening is future (tickets on sale from Monday). A 'has been' and B 'is being' are not coherent. ('is' would be defensible in formal prose but is not offered.)
g-conditional-24.ldbs: L yes (had been / were both fit 'evening ___ a private function'); D yes (the contrary fact 'tickets will be sold to the general public' comes after); B moderate (as though + had been is believed by some mid-level students); S no.
g-conditional-24.why: Medium: L and D pass; B only moderate because as though + were is a drilled form.
g-conditional-24.editorNote: The unreal reading is forced only by the although-clause.

overall: Band counts: easy 0, medium 14, hard 4 (14, 15, 21, 23), i.e. hard is about 22 percent against the 30 percent target; no easy items at all, so the entry-level quota is empty. Items are on the whole similar to or harder than TOEIC conditionals, never easier. Strength: the unit is the real mixed-conditional/inversion material (14, 15, 21 are good). Weaknesses: (1) real vs unreal readings leak in 07, 11, 15, 17; 11 is a real second answer (is + would). (2) Items 18-21 are four consecutive inversion items with the same option set rotated (Should/Were/If/Had), and the answer of one is the distractor of another; also 'unless' is the answer of 08 and a distractor of 09. (3) Items 19 and 20 are weak on B (no distractor a good student believes) and could be sharpened by using a believable near-miss instead of a plain ungrammatical one. (4) Several stems are padded with relative clauses that serve as filler rather than as a lure (20, 19, 18). To reach the hard target, rewrite 18-20 along the lines of 21 (reverse trap) or 14/15 (mixed time reference).
